summary.text: Take \(n=14\): the prime counts in the successive intervals \(((j-1)14,j14]\), for \(j=1,\ldots,14\), are \(6,3,4,3,3,4,2,4,1,4,2,3,3,2\). The only \(1\le k<14\) for which \(2k+1\) is prime are \(k=1,2,3,5,6,8,9,11\), and in every case the \(k\)-th and \((k+1)\)-st entries of this list differ, so no required \(k\) exists.

full_proof.text:
We disprove the strengthened (“moreover”) assertion by taking
\[
n=14.
\]
Since \(14>1\) and \(14\ne 8\), the conjecture would require a positive integer \(k<14\) such that \(2k+1\) is prime and
\[
\pi(14k)-\pi(14(k-1))
=
\pi(14(k+1))-\pi(14k).
\tag{1}
\]
We show that no such \(k\) exists.

For clarity, put
\[
c_j=\pi(14(j+1))-\pi(14j) \qquad (j\geq 0).
\]
Thus \(c_j\) is the number of primes in \((14j,14(j+1)]\). Equation (1) is precisely
\[
c_{k-1}=c_k.
\tag{2}
\]
There is no endpoint ambiguity here: every positive endpoint under consideration is a multiple of \(14\), hence is composite, so using open rather than half-open intervals gives the same prime counts.

We first calculate all the required interval counts. The primes in the successive intervals are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
j & (14j,14(j+1)]\text{ contains the primes} & c_j\\ \hline
0 &(0,14]: 2,3,5,7,11,13 &6\\
1 &(14,28]: 17,19,23 &3\\
2 &(28,42]: 29,31,37,41 &4\\
3 &(42,56]: 43,47,53 &3\\
4 &(56,70]: 59,61,67 &3\\
5 &(70,84]: 71,73,79,83 &4\\
6 &(84,98]: 89,97 &2\\
7 &(98,112]: 101,103,107,109 &4\\
8 &(112,126]: 113 &1\\
9 &(126,140]: 127,131,137,139 &4\\
10 &(140,154]: 149,151 &2\\
11 &(154,168]: 157,163,167 &3\\
12 &(168,182]: 173,179,181 &3\\
13 &(182,196]: 191,193 &2.
\end{array}
\]
These lists are exhaustive by elementary trial division. Indeed, every composite integer at most \(196\) has a prime divisor at most \(\sqrt{196}=14\), so it is enough to test divisibility by \(2,3,5,7,11,13\). Applying those tests to the integers in each displayed interval gives exactly the listed primes. Equivalently, the cumulative prime-counting values at the relevant endpoints are
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrrrrrrrr}
x&0&14&28&42&56&70&84&98&112&126&140&154&168&182&196\\ \hline
\pi(x)&0&6&9&13&16&19&23&25&29&30&34&36&39&42&44.
\end{array}
\]
Taking consecutive differences gives
\[
(c_0,c_1,\ldots,c_{13})
=(6,3,4,3,3,4,2,4,1,4,2,3,3,2).
\tag{3}
\]

Now \(0<k<14\) leaves exactly the thirteen cases \(k=1,2,\ldots,13\). We inspect both necessary conditions—primality of \(2k+1\) and equality of the adjacent counts—in one table:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
k&2k+1&c_{k-1}&c_k&\text{reason the required conjunction fails}\\ \hline
1&3&6&3&6\ne3\\
2&5&3&4&3\ne4\\
3&7&4&3&4\ne3\\
4&9&3&3&9\text{ is composite}\\
5&11&3&4&3\ne4\\
6&13&4&2&4\ne2\\
7&15&2&4&15\text{ is composite}\\
8&17&4&1&4\ne1\\
9&19&1&4&1\ne4\\
10&21&4&2&21\text{ is composite}\\
11&23&2&3&2\ne3\\
12&25&3&3&25\text{ is composite}\\
13&27&3&2&27\text{ is composite}.
\end{array}
\]
For the composite entries one may explicitly note
\[
9=3^2,
\qquad 15=3\cdot5,
\qquad 21=3\cdot7,
\qquad 25=5^2,
\qquad 27=3^3.
\]
Thus those five values of \(k\) fail the condition that \(2k+1\) be prime. For every other possible value, namely
\[
k\in\{1,2,3,5,6,8,9,11\},
\]
(the corresponding values \(2k+1\) are \(3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23\)), the two sides of (1) are the unequal adjacent counts displayed in the table. Hence none of the thirteen possible values of \(k\) satisfies all the required conditions.

Consequently, for \(n=14>1\), with \(14\ne8\), there is no positive integer \(k<14\) for which \(2k+1\) is prime and the two adjacent length-\(14\) intervals have equal prime counts. This directly falsifies the “moreover” clause. Since the stated conjecture universally requires both its positivity clause and this strengthened clause for every \(n\), failure of the strengthened clause at \(n=14\) disproves the whole conjunction, regardless of whether the separate assertion \(a(14)>0\) holds.
